judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's values are right — 13, 16, ones digits 5 and 8 for the 15 and 18 drawings, 14 < 17, order 12/16/19, missing part 7, and a difference of 4 — and verify.json agrees with every one. But the packet contains the exact defect this run's clustering calls verify-every-printed-answer-slot, and the judge scored answer_key_quality and instruction_following 4/4 without finding it. Problems 1 and 2 each print TWO blanks: worksheet.tex lines 39 and 54 both read '$10 \;+\; \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}} \;=\; \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}$', so the child writes the ones digit and then the whole. verify.json gives each problem a single eval for the whole (13 and 16), so the ones digit — the entire point of a 'one ten and some ones' sheet — is never machine-checked, and Quick Answers prints only '1. 13' and '2. 16'. This is the same shape as the confirmed curr-032 example. Two further gaps: problems 3, 4 and 6 require a drawn or marked representation ('Draw 15 counters', 'Mark 16, 12 and 19 on the number line') recorded as machine-verified with no manual entry, and the bank prints '5. —' and '8. —, 4' for the two verified relations.

strengths_to_preserve: Problems 1 and 2 present the identical structure in two materials — a ten-frame plus loose counters, then a ten-stick plus loose cubes — and the key says so rather than leaving the child to notice: 'this is the same idea as problem 1 in a different material. Say the sentence aloud both ways — "ten and six" and "sixteen" — so the number word and the model line up.'

Problem 8 refuses to let the comparison stay qualitative: part (a) asks for the relation and part (b) asks how many more loose cubes, so the child must quantify the gap. The key explains why it is small ('the two tens cancel out') and then defends the slow method too ('A child who tries to subtract nineteen minus fifteen by counting all the cubes will get the same four — slower, but correct. Show them the shortcut afterwards, not instead').

Problem 7 inverts problems 1 and 2 rather than repeating them — the whole is given and a part is missing — and the key names the inversion explicitly ('Same bond, read the other way'), so the number bond is taught as a relationship rather than as a third picture.

The declared trap on problem 3 (writing 15 in the ones box) is the real teen-number error, is machine-proved distinguishable, and the key answers it with a rule the child can apply everywhere: 'The first frame is already used up, so the ones can never be more than nine.'

root_causes.description: Problems 1 and 2 print two response slots and verify one. The worksheet asks the child to complete '10 + __ = __', so there are two answers (3 and 13; 6 and 16), and the answer key prints both — but verify.json holds a single eval per problem for the total, so the ones digit is delivered unchecked and does not appear in the Quick Answers bank. On a sheet whose entire focus is 'representing teen numbers as one ten and some ones', the unverified half is the half the focus names. scripts/verify.py's coverage gate accepts this because it requires only one check per problem id.
evidence: evals/runs/curriculum-shardX-20260803T181926Z/tasks/curr-031/worksheet.tex lines 39 and 54: '$10 \;+\; \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}} \;=\; \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}$' — two blanks per problem.

verify.json ids 1 and 2 hold one entry each: {'type': 'eval', 'expr': '10 + a', 'at': {'a': 3}, 'expected': 13} and the same shape at a=6 expecting 16 — the ones values 3 and 6 are inputs, never checked expecteds.
answer_key.pdf answers both slots in prose ('the ones are 3', 'Put the two parts together: 10 + 3 = 13') while Quick Answers prints only '1. 13' and '2. 16'.
scripts/verify.py coverage gate near line 2015: 'Every worksheet problem needs at least one check' — id-level, so the second blank is structurally invisible.

root_causes.description: Three problems require a drawn or marked representation and are recorded as machine-verified with no manual entry. Problems 3 and 4 instruct 'Draw 15 counters. Fill the first frame all the way up before you start the second one' and 'Draw 18 counters the same way' — the placement discipline is the skill being taught and it is what an adult must actually look at — while the verify entries check only the ones digit. Problem 6 asks the child to 'Mark 16, 12 and 19 on the number line' before writing the order, and only the ordering is checked.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problems 3 and 4: 'Draw 15 counters. Fill the first frame all the way up before you start the second one.' / 'Draw 18 counters the same way. Fill the first frame first.'
worksheet.pdf problem 6: 'Mark 16, 12 and 19 on the number line. Then write the three numbers in order, smallest first.' — verify.json id 6 is a single compare, order 'asc', expected [12, 16, 19].
verify.json contains no entry of type 'manual'; the packet's machine_observation records gate_chain_manual_flags false.

answer_key.pdf grades the drawn placement ('five counters go in the second frame — one row of five, which is easy to see', 'a full top row of five and three underneath'), so the drawing is assessed work, not scaffolding.

root_causes.description: The Quick Answers bank prints '5. —' for the verified relation '<' and '8. —, 4' for problem 8, where part (a)'s verified '>' becomes an em dash sitting immediately beside part (b)'s correctly printed 4. render_quick_answers._fmt formats a string expected through bare sympy.sympify, which raises on '<' and '>', and falls through to the '---' that render_entry also emits for a manual-only problem. There are no manual entries on this sheet, so both dashes are false blanks — and problem 8's row demonstrates the failure inside a single line.
evidence: verify.json id 5 (compare, order 'relation', expected '<') and id 8's first entry (compare, order 'relation', expected '>') are both verified; the id-8 eval expecting 4 prints correctly on the same row.
scripts/render_quick_answers.py _fmt: the isinstance(v, str) branch returns '---' when sympify raises, and render_entry returns the same token for a problem with no expected values.
The key's worked solutions print both relations correctly ('10 + 4 < 10 + 7', '10 + 9 > 10 + 5'), so the loss is confined to the bank.

improvements.title: Coverage gate must count printed answer slots, not problem ids
improvements.proposed_change: scripts/verify.py's coverage gate currently only requires that every id in 1..problem_count has at least one check (see the 'Coverage gap' block near line 2015), which is why a problem printing two blanks passes with one entry. Add a slot-count gate: have tests/check_answer_line.py (it already segments the worksheet .tex by problem via _tex_segments) count the response slots inside each problem's span — \ansblank, \answerline/\ansline, standalone \underline{\hspace{...}} blanks, and lettered parts '(a)'/'(b)' — and fail the build when a problem's slot count exceeds the number of verify entries carrying that id, naming the uncovered slot. Allow an explicit per-problem opt-out field ("slots": N) for the case where two blanks genuinely hold one answer (a restated equation), so the gate is precise rather than merely noisy. State the rule in SKILL.md beside the existing coverage paragraph: one verify entry per printed response, not per problem number. In this case the uncovered slots are the ones-digit blanks in problems 1 and 2 — '10 + __ = __' printed twice with a single verify entry for the total — which is the same shape as the confirmed curr-032 example.
improvements.regression_test: Add a fixture worksheet .tex with a single problem printing '$10 + \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}} = \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}$' and a verify JSON with one eval entry for that id; assert the answer-line gate exits non-zero and names problem 1's second slot. Add the missing entry and assert exit 0. Today the gate passes both, so the first assertion fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes the single largest verification blind spot in the run: any answer the child actually writes down is either machine-checked or explicitly declared manual, and the answer key's bank stops being narrower than the worksheet.
improvements.risk: Medium. Slot detection is heuristic over LaTeX, so it can false-fail sheets that print a blank as scaffolding (a restated equation, a cross-out target). The "slots" opt-out and a fixture suite covering the \ansblank, \answerline and lettered-part shapes keep the false positives bounded; ship the gate as exit 2 (manual review) for one run before making it exit 1 if that risk is judged too high.

improvements.title: An explanation or drawn/marked response must carry a manual verify entry
improvements.proposed_change: SKILL.md already says to reserve 'manual' for genuinely open reasoning and to use it for 'any explanation/reasoning answer', but nothing enforces it, so the instruction loses to the convenience of a single numeric entry. Add a gate (natural home: tests/check_answer_line.py, which already has the per-problem .tex spans) that scans each problem's student-facing prose for open-response imperatives — 'explain', 'tell what ... did wrong', 'show how you know', 'draw', 'circle', 'cross out', 'mark', 'match ... with a line' — and fails when that problem has no entry of type 'manual'. The numeric check stays; the manual entry is ADDED alongside it so the drawn or spoken part is routed to a human instead of being silently counted as verified. In this case the triggers are problems 3 and 4 ('Draw 15 counters. Fill the first frame all the way up before you start the second one') and problem 6 ('Mark 16, 12 and 19 on the number line'), where the key grades the drawn placement but only the resulting number is checked.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture worksheet problem whose text is 'Tell what Ben did wrong both times. Then write the right answer.' paired with a verify JSON holding only an eval entry for that id: assert the gate exits non-zero and names the open-response phrase. Add {'id':N,'type':'manual','desc':...} and assert exit 0 with the run reporting manual-review items. Today both configurations pass, so the first assertion fails before the fix.
improvements.expected_impact: Gate-chain manual flags start telling the truth, final_response.md stops claiming 'nothing is flagged for manual review' on sheets that contain an explanation prompt, and the human reviewer is pointed at exactly the items a machine cannot judge.
improvements.risk: Medium. Keyword scanning over child-facing prose will catch incidental uses ('circle the greater number', where the circle is the same answer as the verified value). Mitigate by requiring the phrase to introduce a response the key grades separately, and by allowing an explicit '"open": false' acknowledgement on the entry so authors can dismiss a false positive deliberately rather than by accident.

improvements.title: Quick Answers must typeset a verified relation instead of the manual-only em dash
improvements.proposed_change: In scripts/render_quick_answers.py, handle relation expecteds before the sympify fallback in _fmt: when a problem entry is type 'compare' with order 'relation', map the expected string '<', '>', '=', '<=', '>=', '!=' onto its LaTeX glyph ($<$, $>$, $=$, $\le$, $\ge$, $\ne$) and, where the compare 'values' are literals, print the resolved comparison (e.g. '$12 < 15$') so the bank row carries the same information as the worked solution. Reserve '---' exclusively for problems whose only entries are type 'manual', and add a build warning when _fmt would emit '---' for a non-manual entry, so a future silent drop is loud. Keep this fix separate from the sympify-sandbox fix (quick-answers-must-not-typeset-python-builtins) — that one must REJECT a non-mathematical object, this one must RENDER a relation.
improvements.regression_test: Add to tests/test_render_quick_answers.py a fixture verify JSON holding one {'id':1,'type':'compare','order':'relation','expected':'<'} entry and one {'id':2,'type':'manual','desc':...} entry, then assert the generated bank contains a typeset '<' on row 1 and '---' on row 2, and that row 1 is not '---'. Today row 1 renders '---' (sympify('<') raises SympifyError and _fmt falls through), so the assertion fails before the fix and passes after. Cases in this run that the test reproduces: curr-031 problem 5, and problem 8 part (a) whose '—' prints beside its own part (b) value on the row '8. —, 4'.
improvements.expected_impact: Every verified inequality/equality answer becomes visible in the answer key's fast-checking bank, and the em dash regains its single meaning ('nobody machine-checked this'), so a grader can tell a verified relation from a genuine manual item at a glance.
improvements.risk: Low. The change is confined to formatting one expected value; existing numeric, list and dict rows are untouched. The only visible difference is that rows previously blank now print a glyph, which can widen a bank column and re-flow column_count — worth asserting the column arithmetic in the same test.

case_summary: A well-designed teen-number packet whose verification does not reach the skill it teaches. The mathematics is right throughout (13, 16, 5 ones, 8 ones, 14<17, 12/16/19, missing part 7, difference 4) and the design is genuinely good: the same structure shown as a ten-frame and as a ten-stick with the key naming the connection, a number bond that inverts the earlier items rather than repeating them, and a closing comparison that has to be quantified. But problems 1 and 2 each print '10 + __ = __' — two blanks — and carry one verify entry for the total, so the ones digit, which is the whole point of 'one ten and some ones', is delivered unchecked and absent from the answer bank. Problems 3, 4 and 6 ask for a drawing or a marked number line that the key explicitly grades, with no manual entry declared anywhere in the file. And the bank prints an em dash for both verified relations, most visibly on the row '8. —, 4', where an unrendered verified '>' sits beside a correctly rendered 4.
